class_2_pinpoint_too_short_for_the_crite.defect: UNSUPPORTED_PROPOSITION / CRITERION_PROPOSITION_MISMATCH -- research-018 C4 asserts the Legislature's broad-construction command, but the pinpoint quote stopped at the 'disturbing increase in lawsuits' sentence and never reached it.

detail.excerpt_before: The Legislature finds and declares that there has been a disturbing increase in lawsuits brought primarily to chill the valid exercise of the constitutional rights of freedom of speech and petition for the redress of grievances.
detail.excerpt_after: The Legislature finds and declares that there has been a disturbing increase in lawsuits brought primarily to chill the valid exercise of the constitutional rights of freedom of speech and petition for the redress of grievances. The Legislature finds and declares that it is in the public interest to encourage continued participation in matters of public significance, and that this participation should not be chilled through abuse of the judicial process. To this end, this section shall be construed broadly.
detail.note: One uninterrupted run of the registry excerpt, extended forward only. No registry edit was needed -- the broad-construction sentence was already inside the stored section 425.16(a) excerpt verbatim. The proposition text was widened to match; criterion C4 is unchanged.

class_3_criterion_grounded_on_the_questi.defect: UNSUPPORTED_PROPOSITION / CRITERION_PROPOSITION_MISMATCH -- research-029 C2 asserted Lippel's due-process holding while its pinpoint quoted only the sentence in which the court POSES the question ('In this action we are asked to decide whether ...').

registry_edit.case: In re Marriage of Lippel (1990) 51 Cal.3d 1160
registry_edit.change: Run 3's START anchor moved backwards inside the SAME uninterrupted passage of the opinion -- from 'We have long interpreted section 580 in accordance with its plain language.' to 'The issue we address is whether due process and section 580 permit ...' -- so the excerpt now carries the court's due-process answer in part II.A. Text was only ADDED: no run was removed or shortened, no ' ... ' join moved, and every proposition excerpt already grounded on this record (research-029-p3/p4, verification-real-006-p1/p2/p3) is still a verbatim substring of the longer excerpt.
registry_edit.text_source: Same CourtListener full text used in the round-1 re-excerpt (REST API v4, token-authenticated, cluster 1442248, html_lawbox); each run re-asserted in code to be a whitespace-normalized substring of that text before the record was written.
registry_edit.aggregator_caveat: Unchanged. Lippel is a pre-archive Supreme Court decision with NO official courts.ca.gov hosting (documented since B8a); the NO_OFFICIAL_HOSTING disclosure stays in discovery_notes and is still surfaced in the reviewer bundle caveat block.

criterion.before: States, on the authority of In re Marriage of Lippel (1990) 51 Cal.3d 1160, that entering a default judgment ordering child support where the dissolution petition served on the respondent did not request it, and no notice of any such request was served, is a denial of due process as embodied in Code of Civil Procedure section 580.
criterion.after: States, on the authority of In re Marriage of Lippel (1990) 51 Cal.3d 1160, that the court answered the due-process question it posed — whether it is a denial of due process, as embodied in Code of Civil Procedure section 580, to enter a default judgment ordering child support where the dissolution petition served on the respondent did not request it and no notice of any such request was served — by concluding that such a default judgment is void for lack of notice and therefore subject to collateral attack: due process forbids entering a judgment against a defendant who was not given proper notice of the existence of the lawsuit and of the specific relief sought in the complaint served on him, and California satisfies those due process requirements in default cases through section 580.
criterion.legal_content: Equivalent. The criterion still requires the answer's legal substance (due-process defect, embodied in section 580, on a petition that never requested support); it now states it in the court's own terms and every clause is quoted underneath it.

propositions.excerpt_before: the sentence posing the question only
propositions.excerpt_after: the same sentence PLUS 'For the reasons that follow, we conclude that such a default judgment is void for lack of notice and therefore subject to collateral attack by the husband.' (one uninterrupted run; the same excerpt verification-real-006-p2 already uses)

propositions.excerpt: It is a fundamental concept of due process that a judgment against a defendant cannot be entered unless he was given proper notice and an opportunity to defend. (U.S. Const., art. XIV; Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank (1950) 339 U.S. 306, 313-315 [94 L.Ed. 865, 872-874, 70 S.Ct. 652].) California satisfies these due process requirements in default cases through section 580.

It is fundamental to the concept of due process that a defendant be given notice of the existence of a lawsuit and notice of the specific relief which is sought in the complaint served upon him. ... The instant case is a prime example of the foregoing; the petition which was served on Ronald sought no monetary relief from him. Therefore, there was no incentive for Ronald to appear and defend. (stored as one uninterrupted run; the ' ... ' here is display elision in this note only)
